mellifluous

meh-LIF-loo-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Mellifluous is sweet or musical to hear; smoothly and pleasantly flowing.

Audiences filled the hall for hours just to hear the soprano's mellifluous rendition of the old ballad.

Example

The radio host's mellifluous voice made even the traffic report sound like a lullaby.

A voice that turns a dry traffic report into something soothing is exactly mellifluous.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

honeyed: Honeyed means sweet-sounding in a way meant to please or persuade -- honeyed words are sugared to win the listener over. Mellifluous praises the sound itself: a voice or melody that pours along smoothly and sweetly, with no hint that the speaker wants something.

euphonious: Euphonious simply means pleasant to hear, a general word for any agreeable sound. Mellifluous is more particular: it pictures sound flowing like honey -- smooth, unbroken, and sweet -- so a single lovely chime can be euphonious while a flowing voice is mellifluous.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

cacophonous: harsh and grating in sound

Where it sits · how sweetly the sound flows — melodic → mellifluous → dulcet

melodic vs. mellifluous: Melodic simply means having a pleasant tune or rhythm, a common musical description; mellifluous specifically evokes a smooth, honey-like flow to a voice or sound.

dulcet vs. mellifluous: Dulcet pushes the sweetness further -- soft, soothing, almost lullaby-like -- while mellifluous emphasizes the smooth, unbroken flow of the sound as much as its sweetness.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — melli

Root — melli: honey (from Latin mel, mellis, 'honey' -- the i is a linking vowel joining it to the next root)

Root — flu

Root — flu: to flow (from Latin fluere, 'to flow')

Suffix — -ous

Suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Mellifluous combines melli ('honey,' from Latin mel, mellis) + flu ('to flow,' from Latin fluere) + -ous -- literally 'flowing with honey,' describing sound as sweet as honey.

Use the root in a new word: fluent

Use the root in a new word: fluent: By eighth grade she was fluent in Portuguese and working on her French.

Word Choice

Mellifluous describes the smooth, sweet sound of a specific voice or piece of music, distinct from "euphony" (taught earlier in this course), which is the more general noun for the pleasing quality of any sound, especially in language.
